speeches.speaker: David Feeney
speeches.brief: The Australian Labor Party opposed the Criminal Code Amendment (Firearms Trafficking) Bill 2015, which proposed mandatory minimum sentences of five years and maximum penalties of 20 years or 5,000 penalty units for firearms trafficking, citing its opposition in principle to mandatory minimum sentencing and the bill's previous rejection in February and August 2015. Labor announced it would not support the bill in its present form, contrasting it with its own 2012 proposal to increase the maximum penalty to life imprisonment.

speeches.speaker: John Cobb
speeches.brief: Support was voiced for the Criminal Code Amendment (Firearms Trafficking) Bill 2015, introducing a mandatory minimum sentence of five years and doubling maximum penalties to 20 years for firearms trafficking. $88 million has been invested in border screening and 535 illegal firearms seized since 2013.

speeches.speaker: Natasha Griggs
speeches.brief: The Criminal Code Amendment (Firearms Trafficking) Bill 2015 introduces a mandatory minimum sentence of five years imprisonment and doubles maximum penalties to 20 years for firearms trafficking offences. The speaker cited multiple firearms incidents in the Northern Territory, including a drive-by shooting at a Rebels motorcycle gang clubhouse and thefts of firearms from homes and a vehicle, to argue that stronger penalties are needed to keep firearms out of the hands of criminals.

speeches.speaker: Ian Goodenough
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Criminal Code Amendment (Firearms Trafficking) Bill 2015, which introduces a mandatory minimum five-year sentence for firearms trafficking and doubles maximum penalties to 20 years imprisonment or 5,000 penalty units. They argued for stronger licensing of firearm owners with background checks and in-person interviews, rather than focusing on firearm characteristics like calibre or magazine capacity.

speeches.speaker: Michael Keenan
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Criminal Code Amendment (Firearms Trafficking) Bill 2015, introducing a mandatory minimum five-year prison sentence and doubling maximum penalties to 20 years for firearms trafficking, with safeguards for defendants under 18 or with cognitive impairment. The bill targets the estimated 250,000 illicit long-arms and 10,000 handguns in Australia.

speeches.speaker: Angus Taylor
speeches.brief: A motion was moved requesting the Senate to resume consideration of 14 specified bills from the previous session, with each request to be conveyed in a separate message. The bills covered water amendment, managed investment trusts, social services, crime commission, deaths registration, tax and superannuation, crowd-sourced funding, firearms trafficking, and parliamentary entitlements.
